auto.title: How a New Muslim Is to Treat Parents Who Are Not Muslim

ruling.hanafi: Kindness to parents who are not Muslim is obligatory — in word, in deed, and in maintaining them when they are in need. They are obeyed in what is no disobedience, and never in unbelief — Sūrat Luqmān, verse 15.
ruling.maliki: Keeping ties with parents who are not Muslim and treating them well — in kindness, in service and in gentleness — is obligatory, and being undutiful to them is forbidden. They are not obeyed if they command unbelief or disobedience, while the duty to keep their company honourably remains.
ruling.shafii: Dutifulness to parents who are not Muslim is obligatory: maintaining them when they are in need, gentleness of speech with them, and praying that they be guided. They are not obeyed in disobedience.
ruling.hanbali: Dutifulness to parents who are not Muslim is obligatory — in kindness, service, gentleness and visiting — and being undutiful to them is forbidden. Their maintenance is not obligatory where the religion differs, and they are not obeyed in disobedience to God: ﴿وَإِن جَاهَدَاكَ عَلَىٰ أَن تُشْرِكَ بِي مَا لَيْسَ لَكَ بِهِ عِلْمٌ فَلَا تُطِعْهُمَا وَصَاحِبْهُمَا فِي الدُّنْيَا مَعْرُوفًا﴾ Sūrat Luqmān, verse 15.

auto.title: Ruling on tahur water altered by an adjacent substance that does not blend

ruling.hanafi: Ablution is valid with water altered by an adjacent substance such as fat, oil, or wax, since change by mere proximity does not strip it of being absolute water.
ruling.maliki: Purification is valid with water altered by an adjacent substance such as fat, oil, or wax; it stays tahur, removing hadath and impurity.
ruling.shafii: Hadath and najasah may be removed with water altered by an adjacent substance such as fat or oil, because the change comes from proximity, not from blending.
ruling.hanbali: Purifying with water altered by an adjacent substance such as fat, oil, or wax is disliked, yet it validly removes hadath because it is still called absolute water.

auto.title: Ruling on tahur water heated by energy, by the sun, or by something impure

ruling.hanafi: Performing the ablution with heated water is permitted without any dislike, whether it was heated by fire or by the sun.
ruling.maliki: Purification is valid without dislike using water heated by fire or by something impure, so long as the smoke of the impurity has not altered it; sun-heated water is disliked in hot lands, a dislike on medical grounds.
ruling.shafii: Purification with heated water is valid; sun-heated water in a beaten-metal vessel in a hot land is disliked when used on the body while still hot, and water heated by fire is not disliked even if the fuel is impure.
ruling.hanbali: Purifying with water heated by something impure, or by the sun when it grows very hot, is disliked, yet hadath is validly removed with it.

auto.title: Ruling on water left over by cats and by smaller roaming animals

ruling.hanafi: Water left over by a cat or a smaller creature is pure, but performing wudu with it is disliked when other water is at hand; if none is, one uses it and does not resort to tayammum.
ruling.maliki: Water left over by a cat or a smaller creature is tahur and removes hadath without any dislike, since such animals are among those that go about among us.
ruling.shafii: Water left over by a cat or a smaller creature such as a mouse is pure and purifying and removes hadath without dislike, on the strength of the hadith about the cat.
ruling.hanbali: Water left over by a cat or a smaller creature is pure and purifying, removes hadath, and its use is not disliked.

auto.title: Ruling when tahur water cannot be told apart from impure water

ruling.hanafi: When tahur water cannot be told from impure water, one weighs the signs for purification and drinking if the greater part is pure; if the two are equal, one performs tayammum.
ruling.maliki: When tahur water cannot be told from water that is impure or made impure, he performs wudu from each vessel and prays after it, praying as many times as there are impure vessels plus one; he does not weigh the signs.
ruling.shafii: One weighs the signs between the two vessels and purifies himself with the one he judges most likely to be pure; he is not obliged to pour the other away.
ruling.hanbali: Using the two indistinguishable vessels is forbidden and he does not weigh probabilities between them, so he performs tayammum, and neither pouring them out nor mixing them is a condition; but if the pure water reaches two qullas and they can be mixed in a vessel that holds them, mixing and using it becomes obligatory.

auto.title: The ruling on purifying with vessels of gold and silver

ruling.hanafi: Using gold and silver vessels for eating, drinking, and purification is forbidden, yet purification from them is valid though sinful.
ruling.maliki: Using and acquiring gold and silver vessels is forbidden, even for a woman, yet purification from them is valid though sinful.
ruling.shafii: Using them for purification and otherwise is forbidden, yet purification with them is valid despite the prohibition.
ruling.hanbali: Using gold and silver vessels for purification and otherwise is forbidden; whoever performs ablution from them, his ablution is valid though sinful.

auto.title: Ruling on Saying the Basmalah at the Beginning of the Ablution

ruling.hanafi: Saying the basmalah at the beginning of the ablution is a sunnah, not an obligation; whoever omits it forgetfully incurs nothing and their ablution is valid.
ruling.maliki: Saying the basmalah at the beginning of the ablution is recommended, not obligatory, and it is recommended during it for one who omitted it at the start and then remembered.
ruling.shafii: Saying the basmalah is a sunnah at the beginning of the ablution, with the wording “Bismillāh al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm”; if omitted deliberately or forgetfully, the ablution is not invalidated.
ruling.hanbali: Saying the basmalah is obligatory in the ablution when one remembers, and it lapses through forgetfulness or ignorance.

auto.title: Ruling on Washing the Hands, for One Newly Woken from the Night's Sleep, Before Putting Them into the Vessel

ruling.hanafi: Washing the hands up to the wrists three times at the start of wudu is a sunnah, more emphasised for one newly woken from sleep, and it is not obligatory.
ruling.maliki: Washing the hands three times before putting them into the vessel is a sunnah in every wudu, as an act of devotion, for one newly woken from sleep and for others alike, and it is not obligatory.
ruling.shafii: It is an emphasised sunnah for one newly woken from the night's sleep to wash the hands three times before putting them into the vessel, and it is not obligatory.
ruling.hanbali: It is obligatory for one newly woken from the night's sleep that breaks the ablution to wash the hands three times before putting them into the vessel, as an act of devotion following the apparent sense of the hadith.

auto.title: Ruling on Washing the Face and the Ruling on Mouth-rinsing and Sniffing Water with it in Ablution

ruling.hanafi: Washing the face is obligatory; rinsing the mouth and the nose are emphasised sunnah in the ablution and obligatory in the full bath. The face extends lengthwise from the usual hairline to the bottom of the chin, and breadthwise from ear to ear.
ruling.maliki: Washing the face is an obligation, and mouth-rinsing and sniffing water are two sunnahs of ablution and not part of its obligations. It is obligatory to cover the entire face with water once.
ruling.shafii: Washing the face is an obligatory pillar of ablution, while mouth-rinsing and sniffing water are two independent sunnahs and not part of the obligations of washing the face; omitting them does not invalidate ablution.
ruling.hanbali: Washing the face is an essential element of ablution, and mouth-rinsing and sniffing water are obligatory as part of washing the face, in both ablution and ghusl; ablution is not valid without them.

auto.title: Ruling on Going to Excess in Rinsing the Mouth and Nose for One Who Is Not Fasting

ruling.hanafi: Going to excess in rinsing the mouth and nose is a sunnah for one who is not fasting: in the mouth it means the water reaching the throat, and in the nose it means reaching the nasal passage.
ruling.maliki: Going to excess in rinsing the mouth and nose is recommended for one who is not fasting, such that the water reaches the furthest part of the mouth and nose without harmful overdoing.
ruling.shafii: Going to excess in rinsing the mouth and nose is a sunnah for one who is not fasting: in the mouth by moving the water around the whole mouth, and in the nose by drawing it in with the breath to the furthest part, based on his saying ﷺ: “And go to excess in sniffing up water, unless you are fasting.”
ruling.hanbali: Going to excess in rinsing the mouth and nose is a sunnah for one who is not fasting, by bringing the water to the furthest part of the mouth and nose, based on the hadith of Laqīṭ ibn Ṣabirah: “And go to excess in sniffing up water, unless you are fasting.”

auto.title: Washing the Arms to the Elbows, and Whether the Elbows Are Included

ruling.hanafi: Washing the arms to the elbows is one of the obligations of the ablution, and the elbows are included in what is washed.
ruling.maliki: Washing the arms together with the elbows is an obligation in the ablution, and the water must cover them entirely.
ruling.shafii: Washing the arms together with the elbows is one of the obligations of the ablution, and including them is required — Sūrat al-Māʾidah, verse 6.
ruling.hanbali: Washing the arms together with the elbows is one of the obligations of the ablution, and the elbows must be included, since the Prophet ﷺ did so in explanation of the verse.

auto.title: The Obligatory Extent of Wiping the Head, and the Ruling on Wiping the Ears with It

ruling.hanafi: What is a farḍ is wiping a quarter of the head, and wiping the ears is an emphasised sunnah, done with the water of the head or with fresh water.
ruling.maliki: It is obligatory to cover the whole head in wiping, once, and wiping the ears is an emphasised sunnah with fresh water.
ruling.shafii: Wiping whatever the name applies to of the head suffices, even a single hair within its limits, and wiping the ears is an independent sunnah with fresh water.
ruling.hanbali: It is obligatory to wipe the whole head together with the ears, since they are part of it, wiped with the water of the head or with fresh water; confining oneself to part of it does not suffice except for one with a valid excuse.

auto.title: Washing the Feet to the Ankles, and Whether the Ankles Are Included

ruling.hanafi: Washing the feet to the ankles is one of the obligations of the ablution, and the ankles — the two bones protruding at the joint of the leg and the foot — are included in what is washed.
ruling.maliki: Washing the feet together with the ankles is an obligation in the ablution, and the water must cover them entirely.
ruling.shafii: Washing the feet together with the ankles is one of the obligations of the ablution, and including them is required — Sūrat al-Māʾidah, verse 6.
ruling.hanbali: Washing the feet together with the ankles is one of the obligations of the ablution, and the ankles must be included, since the Prophet ﷺ did so in explanation of the verse.

auto.title: Washing the Limbs Three Times, and Whether the Head Is Wiped Three Times

ruling.hanafi: Washing the limbs three times — the face, the arms and the feet — is an emphasised sunnah; the head, however, is wiped once, and exceeding three is disliked.
ruling.maliki: Washing the limbs three times — the face, the arms and the feet — is recommended, and exceeding that is disliked; the head is wiped once, and wiping it three times is disliked.
ruling.shafii: Doing all the acts of the ablution three times is a sunnah, both the washing and the wiping: the limbs are washed three times and the head and ears are wiped three times.
ruling.hanbali: Washing the limbs three times — the face, the arms and the feet — is a sunnah, but wiping the head three times is not: it is wiped once, and exceeding three is disliked.

auto.title: Whether the Order of the Limbs in the Ablution Must Be Kept

ruling.hanafi: Keeping the order of the limbs is an emphasised sunnah, not an obligation: if one reverses it — washing the feet before the face — the ablution is valid, though disliked.
ruling.maliki: Keeping the order among the obligatory acts of the ablution is a sunnah: whoever reverses it, his ablution is valid; it is sunnah for him to repeat the reversed act alone if the interval has grown long enough for drying, and otherwise to repeat it together with what follows it.
ruling.shafii: The order is one of the obligations of the ablution and it is not valid without it, since the verse sets it out in sequence; whoever washes a limb out of its place, that washing does not count.
ruling.hanbali: The order is one of the obligations of the ablution and it is not valid without it, on the strength of his saying ﷺ: “Begin with what Allah began with”, related by al-Nasāʾī; whoever departs from it, his ablution is void.

auto.title: Whether the Limbs Must Be Washed Without Interruption

ruling.hanafi: Washing the limbs without interruption is a sunnah, not an obligation: if a limb dries or the interval grows long, the ablution is valid, though disliked if there was no excuse.
ruling.maliki: Washing without interruption is an obligation in the ablution for one who remembers and is able; its measure is that the limb washed before does not dry in a moderate span. If the limbs dry through a long interval, the ablution must be repeated.
ruling.shafii: Washing without interruption is a sunnah in the ablution, not an obligation: the washing of the limbs may be spread out even if the earlier limb dries, and the ablution is valid without it.
ruling.hanbali: Washing without interruption is one of the obligatory acts of the ablution and does not lapse through forgetfulness or ignorance; it means not delaying the washing of a limb until the one before it dries in a moderate span. Drying does no harm if it is due to being occupied with a sunnah or with dispelling misgivings.

auto.title: The Ruling on the Remembrance and Supplication after the Ablution

ruling.hanafi: It is recommended for one who has finished the ablution to say: “I bear witness that there is no god but God alone, having no partner, and I bear witness that Muḥammad is His servant and His messenger. O God, make me of those who turn to You in repentance, and make me of those who keep themselves pure.”
ruling.maliki: The remembrance and supplication after the ablution — the two testimonies and the transmitted supplication — are recommended, and they are among the manners and recommended acts of the ablution.
ruling.shafii: It is a sunnah to say the two testimonies and the transmitted supplication after the ablution, facing the qibla and raising the hands, since it is established in the sunnah.
ruling.hanbali: The remembrance and supplication after the ablution are recommended: the two testimonies, and the words “O God, make me of those who turn to You in repentance, and make me of those who keep themselves pure.”

auto.title: The ruling on intention (niyyah) in ablution and whether it lapses through forgetfulness

ruling.hanafi: A confirmed sunnah and not a condition for the validity of ablution; ablution is valid without intention.
ruling.maliki: An obligation and an essential condition for the validity of ablution; it is invalid without it.
ruling.shafii: The first essential element among the essential elements of ablution; its place is the heart at washing the first part of the face.
ruling.hanbali: A condition for the validity of every purification from ritual impurity — ablution, full bath, and dry ablution; it does not lapse whether by forgetfulness or deliberately.

auto.title: One Whose Ablution Breaks During the Prayer: Does He Continue or Start Again?

ruling.hanafi: One overtaken by impurity during his prayer without intent may purify and continue from where he was, provided he does nothing incompatible with prayer other than walking to purify; starting again is better.
ruling.maliki: The prayer is void by impurity, whether deliberate, forgetful or involuntary; he must purify and start the prayer again from the beginning, and may not continue.
ruling.shafii: His prayer is void by impurity, whether deliberate, forgetful or involuntary; he must purify and start the prayer again from the beginning, and does not continue from where he was.
ruling.hanbali: The prayer is void by impurity, whether deliberate, forgetful or involuntary; he must perform ablution and start the prayer again from the beginning, and continuing is not valid.

auto.title: One Who Forgot He Was Impure, Prayed, and Then Remembered

ruling.hanafi: His prayer is void, and he must repeat it after purifying — whether he remembered within the time or after it — since purity is a condition that forgetfulness does not lift.
ruling.maliki: His prayer is void, and he must repeat it whenever he remembers, even after the time has passed, since purity from impurity is a condition of validity that forgetfulness does not lift.
ruling.shafii: His prayer is void, and he must make it up whenever he remembers, on the strength of his saying ﷺ: “No prayer is accepted without purity”; forgetfulness lifts the sin but does not make the prayer valid.
ruling.hanbali: His prayer is void, and he must repeat it whenever he remembers, on the strength of his saying ﷺ: “Whoever forgets a prayer or sleeps through it, let him pray it when he remembers it”; a condition is not lifted by forgetfulness.

auto.title: The Full Bath of a Woman after Menstruation or Post-natal Bleeding Ends

ruling.hanafi: The full bath becomes obligatory once the bleeding ends — either by reaching its maximum term or by the sign of purity, dryness or the white discharge — and the bath must cover the whole body with water, together with rinsing the mouth and the nose.
ruling.maliki: The full bath becomes obligatory once the bleeding has wholly ceased and the sign of purity is seen; in it, covering the whole body with water together with rubbing, continuity when one remembers and is able, and running the water through the hair are obligatory.
ruling.shafii: The full bath becomes obligatory once the bleeding ends and purity is seen; the whole body must be covered with water down to the roots of the hair, with the intention of lifting the major impurity of menstruation or post-natal bleeding.
ruling.hanbali: The full bath becomes obligatory once the bleeding of menstruation or of childbirth has ended and purity is established by the white discharge or by dryness; the whole body must be covered with water, and the hair must be undone for the bath of menstruation and post-natal bleeding, unlike the bath of janābah when the roots are soaked.

auto.title: What the Full Bath Requires for It to Suffice

ruling.hanafi: The obligations of the full bath are three: rinsing the mouth, rinsing the nose, and covering the whole body with water, including what lies beneath the hair. The intention is a sunnah, not a condition of its validity.
ruling.maliki: The obligations of the full bath are: the intention at its beginning, continuity, covering the outer body with water, rubbing, and running the water through the hair. Rinsing the mouth and the nose is not obligatory in it; both are sunnah.
ruling.shafii: The two essentials of the full bath are: the intention, at the washing of the first part of the body, and covering the whole body with water, both hair and skin. Rinsing the mouth and the nose is not obligatory in it.
ruling.hanbali: The obligation of the full bath is to cover the whole body with water, with the intention; and rinsing the mouth and the nose, and bringing the water beneath the hair however thick it is, are obligatory with it.

auto.title: The Complete Form of the Full Bath, after the Practice of the Prophet ﷺ

ruling.hanafi: He begins by washing his hands three times, then removes any filth on his body, then performs the ablution as for prayer — delaying the washing of the feet if he is standing in gathered water — then pours water over his head three times, then over his right side and then his left, covering the body and rubbing it.
ruling.maliki: It is sunnah that he begin by washing his hands, and recommended that he remove any filth on his body, then wash the parts of the ablution completely once, then pour water over his head three times, beginning with the upper body and the right side. Rubbing and keeping the washing continuous are obligatory in it.
ruling.shafii: Its transmitted form: he washes his hands, removes any filth on his body, performs the ablution as for prayer, works his fingers into the roots of his hair until they are wetted, pours water over his head three times, then covers the rest of his body beginning with the right side, rubbing and keeping the washing continuous.
ruling.hanbali: The sunnah is that he begin by washing his hands, then wash his private parts and whatever filth is on them, then perform the ablution as for prayer, then pour three handfuls over his head, wetting the roots of the hair, then pour water over the rest of his body beginning with the right side, rubbing what he can and keeping the washing continuous.

auto.title: The ruling on tayammum when water is present but there is fear of using it

ruling.hanafi: Tayammum is permitted despite water being present if one fears harm from using it due to illness or severe cold that risks death or worsening sickness.
ruling.maliki: Tayammum is permitted for the sick and for whoever fears worsening illness, delayed recovery, or death from using water.
ruling.shafii: Tayammum is permitted despite water's presence for one who fears, from using it, loss of life or of a limb's function, and likewise delayed recovery or a gross disfigurement on an exposed part of the body, established by a trustworthy physician or experience. Severe cold is treated like illness.
ruling.hanbali: Tayammum is permissible despite water's presence if one fears bodily harm from using it due to illness or severe cold, being unable to warm the water or avert its harm.

auto.title: What the Dry Ablution May Be Performed With: Earth and What Lies on Its Surface

ruling.hanafi: The dry ablution is valid with anything pure of the earth's kind — earth, sand, stone, gypsum — whether it carries dust or not.
ruling.maliki: The dry ablution is valid with anything lying on the surface of the earth that is of its kind and unaltered by manufacture — earth, sand, gravel, stones — and dust is not required.
ruling.shafii: The dry ablution is valid only with pure unmixed earth carrying dust that clings to the hand; it is not valid with smooth stone, nor with sand that carries no dust.
ruling.hanbali: It is a condition that the dry ablution be with pure earth carrying dust that clings to the hand — Sūrat al-Māʾidah, verse 6.

auto.title: The Form of the Dry Ablution and How Many Strikes It Takes

ruling.hanafi: The dry ablution is two strikes: one with which he wipes his whole face, and one with which he wipes his arms including the elbows; both are obligatory.
ruling.maliki: What is obligatory is one strike with which he wipes his face and his hands to the wrists; a second strike, wiping from the wrists to the elbows, is a sunnah.
ruling.shafii: The dry ablution is two strikes and no fewer: one for the face and one for the arms including the elbows; and the earth must be transferred by the strike or by what stands in its place.
ruling.hanbali: What is obligatory is a single strike with which he wipes his face and his hands — on the strength of the hadith of ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir: “It would have sufficed you to strike the earth with your hands, then blow, then wipe your face and your hands with them.”

auto.title: The Intention for the Dry Ablution: Does It Lift Impurity or Only Permit the Prayer?

ruling.hanafi: The dry ablution lifts the impurity so long as the excuse remains; he intends by it purification from impurity or the permitting of prayer, and with it he prays whatever obligatory and voluntary prayers he wishes.
ruling.maliki: The dry ablution permits the prayer and does not lift the impurity; the intention of lifting impurity is therefore not valid, and he intends instead the permitting of the prayer or of what the impurity barred.
ruling.shafii: The dry ablution permits the prayer and does not lift the impurity; he intends the permitting of an obligatory prayer, so as to pray one obligatory prayer and whatever voluntary prayers he wishes, and the intention of lifting impurity is not valid.
ruling.hanbali: The dry ablution permits the prayer while the impurity remains; he intends the permitting of the prayer, or of an act of worship that requires purity — and if he intends the lifting of impurity, his dry ablution is not valid.

auto.title: How Many Obligatory Prayers May Be Prayed with One Dry Ablution

ruling.hanafi: With his dry ablution he prays whatever obligatory and voluntary prayers he wishes, since it lifts the impurity; it is void only by a nullifier or by his becoming able to use water.
ruling.maliki: With one dry ablution he prays only one obligatory prayer, and he performs it anew for each prescribed prayer; he may pray with it the voluntary prayers attached to that one.
ruling.shafii: He does not join two obligatory prayers on one dry ablution; he performs it for each obligatory prayer, and with it may pray whatever voluntary prayers he wishes before and after.
ruling.hanbali: The dry ablution is bound to the prayer time: within that time he prays with it whatever obligatory and voluntary prayers he wishes, and it is void once the time of the prayer he performed it for has gone.

auto.title: How Far One Must Search for Water Before the Dry Ablution

ruling.hanafi: Searching for water is required only if he strongly supposes there is water near him, less than a mile off; he then searches as far as a bowshot, without going as far as a mile. If he has no such supposition, he performs the dry ablution without searching.
ruling.maliki: If he is certain there is no water, he does not search; if he is in doubt, he must search what is near him; and if he is certain it is there, he must go for it, so long as the prayer time does not run out and he does not fear for himself.
ruling.shafii: If he is certain there is no water, he performs the dry ablution without searching; if he merely supposes there may be some, the search is required once the prayer time has come in — in his baggage, among his companions and around him, within the reach of a call, as far as a voice carries. If he knows of water within the nearer distance, he must go to it, if he is safe as to himself and his property.
ruling.hanbali: He must search for water in his baggage, among his companions, and in what is customarily near him; if he finds none, or fears the prayer time will pass or that he will come to harm, he performs the dry ablution and need not go far.

auto.title: A Woman Who Becomes Pure before the Prayer's Time Ends

ruling.hanafi: A woman whose bleeding stops at the full ten days with as much time left as suffices for the opening takbīr must perform the prayer; if it stops before ten days, the prayer is due of her only if enough time remains for her to bathe and pronounce the opening takbīr.
ruling.maliki: The prayer is due of her if, after her purification, enough of its time remains for one complete unit.
ruling.shafii: A woman who becomes pure with as much of the time left as suffices for one takbīr must perform that prayer.
ruling.hanbali: A woman who becomes pure before the time ends, even by as much as the opening takbīr, must perform that prayer together with the prayer that may be combined with it before it.

auto.title: Whether a Woman Who Becomes Pure Late in the Day Must Also Pray the Earlier of the Two Joinable Prayers

ruling.hanafi: Only the prayer in whose time she became pure is due of her; she does not pray ẓuhr with ʿaṣr nor maghrib with ʿishāʾ, since the earlier prayer's time ended while she was still menstruating and not addressed by it.
ruling.maliki: Ẓuhr and ʿaṣr are due of her if she becomes pure when enough time remains before sunset for purification and five rakʿahs, and maghrib and ʿishāʾ if enough remains before dawn for purification and four rakʿahs; otherwise only the latter prayer is due. Both are performed on time, not made up, since this is their necessary time.
ruling.shafii: Ẓuhr is due with ʿaṣr if she becomes pure during ʿaṣr, and maghrib with ʿishāʾ if during ʿishāʾ, because in a state of excuse the time of the second serves the first, as in joining prayers.
ruling.hanbali: Ẓuhr is due with ʿaṣr if she becomes pure during ʿaṣr, and maghrib with ʿishāʾ if during ʿishāʾ, because in a state of excuse their two times become one.

auto.title: A Prayer Whose Time Had Begun When Menstruation Set In Before It Was Performed

ruling.hanafi: She does not make it up, since the obligation only settles at the end of the time; if she menstruated within it, it fell from her.
ruling.maliki: She does not make it up if she menstruated within the extended time — unless she had delayed it until the time no longer sufficed to perform it with her purification, in which case she makes it up.
ruling.shafii: She makes it up if enough of the time had passed to accommodate the prayer and her purification, and she was able to perform it but did not.
ruling.hanbali: She makes it up if, before menstruating, she caught as much of its time as the opening takbīr, since the prayer is caught by the opening takbīr within its time.

auto.title: The Fast of a Woman Who Becomes Pure Before Dawn but Bathes Only After It

ruling.hanafi: Her fast is valid if the bleeding stopped before dawn: if it stopped at the full ten days it is valid even with no time left for the bath, but if before ten, enough of the night must remain for the bath and the opening takbīr.
ruling.maliki: Her fast is valid if the bleeding stopped before dawn even if she delayed the bath until after it, since purity from major impurity is a condition of prayer, not of fasting.
ruling.shafii: Her fast is valid if the bleeding stopped before dawn and she intended the fast, even if she delayed the bath, since the condition of the fast is that the bleeding stop before dawn, not that she bathe before it.
ruling.hanbali: Her fast is valid if the bleeding stopped before dawn and she intended the fast, even if she bathed only after it; her case is that of one in major impurity who begins the day fasting and bathes afterwards.

auto.title: When a Woman Resumes Prayer and Fasting After Becoming Pure

ruling.hanafi: She resumes fasting once the bleeding stops before dawn, and the bath is not a condition for it if the stop came at the full ten days; if earlier, enough of the night must remain for the bath and the opening takbīr. Prayer, however, she resumes only after the bath, or dry ablution when unable.
ruling.maliki: She resumes fasting as soon as she sees the sign of purity before dawn, with no bath required for it; she resumes prayer upon purity, but its performance waits on the bath, and if the time is short she bathes and prays at once.
ruling.shafii: She resumes fasting once the bleeding stops before dawn, with the intention, even if she delays the bath; prayer becomes due upon her at purity if time for a takbīr remains, and she prays as soon as she has bathed.
ruling.hanbali: She resumes fasting upon purity before dawn, with the intention, and delaying the bath does no harm — as with one in major impurity; prayer becomes due upon purity if time for the opening takbīr remains, and she must hasten to bathe so as to pray within the time.

auto.title: Ruling on Tathwīb in the Fajr Adhān

ruling.hanafi: Tathwīb (saying prayer is better than sleep) is recommended in the Fajr call to prayer.
ruling.maliki: It is recommended to say the tathwīb — “Prayer is better than sleep” — twice in the adhān of the dawn prayer specifically, and not in that of any other prayer.
ruling.shafii: Tathwīb is sunnah in the call for the Morning prayer, whether before or after dawn.
ruling.hanbali: The tathwīb is sunnah in the call to prayer for Fajr, even if it is given before dawn, and it is disliked in any other.

auto.title: The Wording of the Iqāmah and the Ruling on Saying Its Phrases Once

ruling.hanafi: The iqāmah is said twice over, like the adhān, with “qad qāmat al-ṣalāh” added twice, making seventeen phrases; saying its phrases once is disliked.
ruling.maliki: All the phrases of the iqāmah are said once, making ten phrases, including “qad qāmat al-ṣalāh” once; only the takbīr at its beginning and end is said twice.
ruling.shafii: The phrases of the iqāmah are said once, making eleven phrases, except the takbīr at its beginning and end and “qad qāmat al-ṣalāh”, which are said twice.
ruling.hanbali: The phrases of the iqāmah are said once, making eleven phrases, except the takbīr at its beginning and end and “qad qāmat al-ṣalāh”, which are said twice, based on the hadith of Anas: “Bilāl was ordered to make the adhān in pairs and the iqāmah singly.”

auto.title: Ruling on the Five Obligatory Prayers and Their Legal Basis

ruling.hanafi: The five prayers are a personal obligation upon every sane, adult Muslim, established by the text of the Qurʾān and the mutawatir sunnah.
ruling.maliki: The five prayers are a personal obligation upon every accountable individual, obligated by definitive text from the Qurʾān and sunnah, with no disagreement among Muslims on the basis of their obligation.
ruling.shafii: The five prayers are among the pillars of Islam, a personal obligation established by the text of the Qurʾān, the sunnah, and the consensus of the nation.
ruling.hanbali: The five prayers are a personal obligation established by the text of the Qurʾān, the sunnah, and the consensus of Muslims, the greatest pillar of Islam after the two testimonies.

auto.title: The Times in Which Prayer Is Forbidden, and How Many They Are

ruling.hanafi: The forbidden times are three, prohibitively disliked: at sunrise until the sun has risen, at its zenith until it declines, and at its yellowing until it sets — except that day's ʿaṣr; and voluntary prayer is disliked after the fajr and the ʿaṣr prayers.
ruling.maliki: Voluntary prayer is prohibited at sunrise, at sunset, and during the Friday sermon; it is disliked after the fajr prayer until the sun has risen the height of a spear, and after the obligatory ʿaṣr until the maghrib is prayed.
ruling.shafii: The forbidden times are five: after the ṣubḥ prayer until the sun has risen the height of a spear, at the zenith except on Friday, after the ʿaṣr prayer until it sets, at sunrise, and at sunset; and the dislike applies to prayer that has no occasioning cause or whose cause comes after it, not to prayer whose cause precedes or accompanies it, such as a missed prayer, the eclipse prayer, and the greeting of the mosque.
ruling.hanbali: The forbidden times are three in outline and five in detail: from the second (true) dawn until the sun has risen the height of a spear, at its standing still until it declines, and from the ʿaṣr prayer until it sets; in them it is permissible to make up obligatory prayers, to pray the two units of the circumambulation, and to repeat a prayer in congregation, and the sunnah of fajr before the obligatory prayer is excepted.

auto.title: The Extent of a Man's ʿAwrah in the Prayer

ruling.hanafi: A man's ʿawrah in the prayer is from below the navel to below the knee; the knee is part of the ʿawrah and the navel is not.
ruling.maliki: A man's grave ʿawrah is the two private parts, and the lighter ʿawrah is what lies between the navel and the knee; the prayer is invalidated by uncovering the grave, while uncovering the lighter is disliked; he repeats the prayer within its time for uncovering the buttocks or part of them, but not for uncovering the thigh.
ruling.shafii: A man's ʿawrah in the prayer is what lies between the navel and the knee; neither the navel nor the knee is part of it, and part of each must be covered so that what lies between them is certainly covered.
ruling.hanbali: The ʿawrah of an adult man in the prayer is what lies between the navel and the knee, neither of which is part of it; and in an obligatory prayer covering one of the shoulders is also obligatory when he is able.

auto.title: Ruling on the awrah of a free adult woman in prayer

ruling.hanafi: The awrah of a free woman in prayer is her whole body except the face, the hands, and the feet; her prayer is valid with these uncovered.
ruling.maliki: Her awrah is her whole body except the face and the hands; uncovering the feet or the hair does not invalidate the prayer, though it is repeated within its time because they are part of the lighter ʿawrah.
ruling.shafii: Her awrah is her whole body except the face and the hands, their backs and palms alike, up to the wrists.
ruling.hanbali: A free adult woman is entirely awrah in prayer except her face, so she must cover her hands and her feet.

auto.title: Ruling on facing the Kaaba itself when near and its direction when far

ruling.hanafi: One who sees the Kaaba must face its very structure; one absent from it must face its direction, and a slight deviation does not harm him.
ruling.maliki: One who sees it must face it exactly, and the distant must face its direction; his prayer is not void by a slight turn to right or left.
ruling.shafii: Facing the Kaaba itself is required with certainty from one who sees it, and by reasoned effort from one far away; aiming at the direction alone does not suffice him.
ruling.hanbali: One who sees it must face it exactly and one far away its direction; a slight deviation does not void the prayer, on the hadith «What lies between east and west is a qibla» — meaning that what lies between the two edges of the direction suffices for one whose qibla falls between them, so it is reckoned in each land according to the direction of its qibla.

auto.title: The Ruling on One Who Prays by Best Judgement and Then Learns He Faced the Wrong Direction

ruling.hanafi: Whoever seeks out the direction of the qibla by his best judgement and prays, then learns of his error, his prayer is valid and no repetition is due, for he did what lay within his capacity.
ruling.maliki: Whoever uses his best judgement and prays, then learns of his error, his prayer suffices and no repetition is due once the time has passed; repeating it within the time is recommended.
ruling.shafii: Whoever prays by his best judgement and then becomes certain of the error must repeat the prayer, within its time and after it, because facing the qibla is a condition that has been shown not to have been met.
ruling.hanbali: One who knows the indications of the qibla, uses his best judgement while travelling and prays, then learns of his error, his prayer is valid and no repetition is due, on the strength of His saying: ﴿فَأَيْنَمَا تُوَلُّوا فَثَمَّ وَجْهُ اللَّهِ﴾ (al-Baqarah 115) and the hadith of ʿĀmir ibn Rabīʿah. But if he prayed while resident and erred, he repeats it.

auto.title: Whether the Intention Must Coincide with the Opening Takbīr

ruling.hanafi: The intention need not coincide with the opening takbīr; it is valid for it to precede the takbīr by a short while, so long as no extraneous act such as speech or eating comes between them.
ruling.maliki: The intention must coincide with the takbīr, or precede it by a very short span joined to it; if it precedes by a long span or an interruption occurs, the prayer is not valid.
ruling.shafii: The intention must coincide with the opening takbīr: it must accompany the beginning of the takbīr and be sustained to its end.
ruling.hanbali: The intention need not coincide with the opening takbīr; it may precede it by a short while so long as he does not revoke it, and coinciding with the takbīr is better.

auto.title: The Ruling on Uttering the Intention with the Tongue

ruling.hanafi: The seat of the intention is the heart, and uttering it with the tongue is recommended, so that the heart's resolve is joined to the tongue's act, and to keep intrusive thoughts at bay.
ruling.maliki: The seat of the intention is the heart, and uttering it is contrary to what is preferable, since it is not established from the Prophet ﷺ; it is recommended only for one afflicted with obsessive doubt, to drive that doubt away.
ruling.shafii: It is a sunnah to utter the intention quietly before the takbīr, so that the tongue assists the heart and the intention is present in all its parts at the opening takbīr.
ruling.hanbali: The seat of the intention is the heart, and uttering it quietly is recommended so that the tongue agrees with the heart; saying it aloud is not prescribed in any case.

auto.title: One Who Cannot Cover His ʿAwrah in the Prayer

ruling.hanafi: It is recommended that he pray seated, gesturing for the bowing and the prostration, since covering the ʿawrah by sitting is better; he may also pray standing with bowing and prostration, and he does not repeat the prayer.
ruling.maliki: He must pray uncovered and standing, with a full bowing and prostration, and he repeats the prayer within its time if he finds a covering.
ruling.shafii: He prays uncovered and standing if he is able, with a full bowing and prostration, and he does not repeat the prayer, for he performed what was required of him in his condition.
ruling.hanbali: It is recommended that he pray uncovered and seated, gesturing for the bowing and the prostration, since covering his ʿawrah by sitting is better; if he prays standing with bowing and prostration, that is permissible, and he does not repeat the prayer.

auto.title: One Who Has Only an Impure Garment

ruling.hanafi: If a quarter of it or more is pure, he must pray in it and may not pray uncovered; if less than a quarter is pure, he may choose between praying in it and praying uncovered, though praying in it is better.
ruling.maliki: He prays in it and does not repeat the prayer if the time is short; repeating it within the time is recommended if the time is ample.
ruling.shafii: He does not pray in the impure garment; rather, he prays uncovered, performing all the pillars in full, and need not repeat the prayer.
ruling.hanbali: He prays in it and does not pray uncovered, and he must repeat the prayer, because the purity of the garment is a condition he did not fulfil.

auto.title: Ruling on Raising Hands During Takbeer and its Places in Prayer

ruling.hanafi: Raises the hands until the thumbs are level with the earlobes at the opening takbīr, and does not raise them at the bowing or at rising from it; within the prayer they are also raised for the takbīr of the qunūt in witr and for the takbīrs of the two ʿĪds.
ruling.maliki: The hands are raised to shoulder level only at the opening takbīr, and raising them at the other descents and risings is disliked.
ruling.shafii: Recommended to raise hands to shoulder level in four positions: Opening, Bowing, Rising from Bowing, and Standing from 1st Tashahhud.
ruling.hanbali: Recommended to raise hands to shoulders or the tops of the ears in three positions: Opening Takbeer, Bowing, and Rising from Bowing.

auto.title: Ruling on the wording of the opening takbir and what may replace it

ruling.hanafi: The prayer is entered with any wording of pure magnification, such as «Allāhu akbar», «Allāhu al-aʿẓam», or «al-ḥamdu lillāh»; the takbir wording is not required.
ruling.maliki: The opening takbir is restricted to the wording «Allāhu akbar» alone, and the prayer is not entered with any other wording.
ruling.shafii: The wording is restricted to «Allāhu akbar» or «Allāhu al-akbar»; no other remembrance and no translation suffices for one able to say it.
ruling.hanbali: The wording «Allāhu akbar» alone suffices; no other remembrance and no translation takes its place for one able to say it.

auto.title: Position of Hands While Standing in Prayer (Qabd vs Sadl)

ruling.hanafi: Recommended for men to place the right hand over the left below the navel; women place them on the chest.
ruling.maliki: The hands are let down, that is, left hanging at the sides, in the obligatory prayer; clasping them in it is disliked if support is intended, and it is permitted in voluntary prayer.
ruling.shafii: It is sunnah to place the right palm over the back of the left hand, below the chest and above the navel, inclined slightly to the left, for both men and women.
ruling.hanbali: Recommended to place the right hand over the left wrist and place them below the navel.

auto.title: The Wording of the Opening Supplication and the Ruling on Saying It Aloud

ruling.hanafi: The wording is: “Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise; blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You.” Saying it silently is a sunnah for the imam, the follower and one praying alone, and saying it aloud is disliked.
ruling.maliki: The opening supplication is disliked in the obligatory prayer, and the recitation begins straight after the takbīr; it is permissible in voluntary prayer.
ruling.shafii: The wording is: “I have turned my face to Him who originated the heavens and the earth, upright and submitting, and I am not of those who associate.” Saying it silently is a sunnah for all who pray, in both the silent and the audible prayers.
ruling.hanbali: The wording is: “Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise; blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You.” Saying it silently is always a sunnah for the imam, the follower and one praying alone, since saying it aloud was not transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ or his Companions.

auto.title: Whether the Basmalah Is Part of al-Fātiḥah, and the Ruling on Saying It Aloud

ruling.hanafi: The basmalah is not a verse of al-Fātiḥah; reciting it silently before al-Fātiḥah in every unit is a sunnah for the imam and one praying alone, and it is said silently even in the audible prayer.
ruling.maliki: Reciting the basmalah and the taʿawwudh before al-Fātiḥah or the sūrah in the obligatory prayer is disliked, whether silently or aloud, for the imam, the follower and one praying alone; in voluntary prayer it is permissible.
ruling.shafii: The basmalah is a full verse of al-Fātiḥah, so reciting it with the sūrah is obligatory for the prayer's validity; it is said aloud in the audible prayer and silently in the silent one.
ruling.hanbali: The basmalah is not part of al-Fātiḥah; reciting it silently before it in every unit is a sunnah for the imam and one praying alone, and saying it aloud is not a sunnah.

auto.title: Ruling on the Follower Reciting al-Fātiḥah Behind the imam in the Silent and the Audible Prayer

ruling.hanafi: Prohibitively disliked (makrūh taḥrīman) for the follower to recite Fatiha behind imam in both silent and loud prayers; imam's recitation suffices.
ruling.maliki: It is recommended for the follower to recite al-Fātiḥah in the silent prayer, and it is disliked in the audible one, even if he cannot hear the imam's recitation.
ruling.shafii: Recitation of Al-Fatiha is an absolute obligation upon the follower in every rakʿah, silent or loud.
ruling.hanbali: Recommended in silent prayers and during imam's pauses in loud prayers; not obligatory. If the imam does not pause, he listens.

auto.title: Ruling on reciting a sura after al-Fatiha in the prayer

ruling.hanafi: Reciting a sura after al-Fatiha is obligatory in the first two units of an obligatory prayer and in every unit of voluntary prayer and witr; in the last two units one may choose.
ruling.maliki: Reciting a sura after al-Fatiha in the first two units is a stressed sunnah; it is disliked in the last two and not prescribed in the funeral prayer.
ruling.shafii: Reciting the sura after al-Fatiha in the first two units is a sunnah for one praying alone, for the imam, and for the follower where the recitation is silent; it is not called for in the last two.
ruling.hanbali: Reciting a sura after al-Fatiha in the first two units is a sunnah; it is not a sunnah in the last two, though if he recites there it is permissible and not disliked; and it is a sunnah for the follower in the silent prayers but not the audible ones.

auto.title: The Ruling on Saying Āmīn and on Saying It Aloud after al-Fātiḥah

ruling.hanafi: Saying āmīn is a sunnah for the imam, the follower and one praying alone after al-Fātiḥah, and saying it silently is a sunnah in both the audible and the silent prayer.
ruling.maliki: Saying āmīn silently is recommended for the follower and one praying alone; the imam says it silently in the silent prayer and does not say it in the audible prayer.
ruling.shafii: Saying āmīn is a sunnah for the imam, the follower and one praying alone after al-Fātiḥah; it is said aloud by all in the audible prayer and silently in the silent one.
ruling.hanbali: Saying āmīn is a sunnah for the imam, the follower and one praying alone; the imam and the follower say it aloud in the audible prayer, on the strength of the hadith of Wāʾil ibn Ḥujr, and silently in the silent prayer.

auto.title: The Least Bending That Suffices for the Bowing

ruling.hanafi: The least that suffices is to bend such that, were he to stretch out his hands, they would reach his knees, or that he be nearer to bowing than to standing.
ruling.maliki: The least that suffices is to bend until his palms come near his knees, were he to place them; levelling the back belongs to perfection and is not a condition.
ruling.shafii: For one of ordinary build, the least that suffices is to bend such that his palms would reach his knees were he to intend placing them upon them, without bending his knees.
ruling.hanbali: For one standing, the least that suffices is to bend until his hands would touch his knees were he to place them upon them; levelling the back is a sunnah, not a condition.

auto.title: Ruling on Shortening Four-Unit Prayers for the Traveler

ruling.hanafi: Shortening four-unit prayers is obligatory for the traveler; completing them is prohibitively disliked provided he sat for the first sitting (otherwise his obligatory prayer is not valid).
ruling.maliki: Shortening four-unit prayers during travel is an emphasised sunnah, superior to completing them.
ruling.shafii: Shortening is a permitted concession for the traveler once his journey reaches two stages; completing the prayer is better, unless it reaches three stages or more, in which case shortening is better.
ruling.hanbali: Shortening is a concession and is superior to completing; if he completes the prayer, that is permissible and not disliked.

auto.title: Ruling on Fasting the Month of Ramadan and Its Legal Basis

ruling.hanafi: Fasting Ramadan is a personal obligation upon every sane, adult, resident, able Muslim, established by the text of the Qurʾān and the mutawatir sunnah.
ruling.maliki: Fasting Ramadan is a personal obligation upon every accountable individual, obligated by definitive text from the Qurʾān and sunnah, with no disagreement among Muslims on the basis of its obligation.
ruling.shafii: Fasting Ramadan is among the pillars of Islam, a personal obligation established by the text of the Qurʾān, the sunnah, and the consensus of the nation.
ruling.hanbali: Fasting Ramadan is a personal obligation established by the text of the Qurʾān, the sunnah, and the consensus of Muslims, one of the five pillars of Islam.

auto.title: Ruling on Completing Shaʿbān Thirty Days if the Crescent is Blocked on the Thirtieth Night

ruling.hanafi: If the crescent is obscured on the thirtieth night of Shaʿbān, it is obligatory to complete Shaʿbān as thirty days. The day of doubt is fasted only as a voluntary fast; fasting it for another obligatory fast is disliked, and fasting it decisively as Ramadan is prohibitively disliked.
ruling.maliki: It is obligatory to complete Shaʿbān thirty days if clouds or dust obstruct sighting the crescent on the thirtieth night. Fasting the day of doubt as a precaution for Ramadan is disliked and does not count for it, while fasting it by habit, voluntarily, or as a make-up fast is permissible.
ruling.shafii: If clouds or dust obstruct sighting the crescent on the thirtieth night of Shaʿbān, completing the month as thirty days is obligatory, based on the Prophet's saying: "If it is obscured, then estimate for it."
ruling.hanbali: If clouds or dust obstruct the thirtieth night of Shaʿbān, it is obligatory to fast it with the intention of Ramadan out of precaution, and completing Shaʿbān as thirty days is not obligatory.

auto.title: Ruling on Using Astronomical Calculation to Confirm the Month of Ramadan

ruling.hanafi: Astronomical calculation is not relied upon to confirm crescents; rather, the standard is visual sighting based on the Prophet's saying: "Fast upon seeing it and break fast upon seeing it," and the words of astronomers are disregarded.
ruling.maliki: The statements of calculators are ignored, and astronomical calculations are not used to establish Ramadan; legal demands are linked to visual sighting or completing the count.
ruling.shafii: Ramadan is not established for people at large by astronomical calculation or by an astrologer's word, but by sighting or by completing Shaʿbān as thirty days; the calculator himself, however, may act on his own calculation, and it counts for his obligatory fast.
ruling.hanbali: Astronomical calculation is not relied upon to establish the entry of Ramadan; fasting becomes obligatory by sighting the crescent, or by completing Shaʿbān as thirty days when the sky is clear. If clouds or haze obscure the crescent on the night of the thirtieth, fasting that day is obligatory.

auto.title: Ruling on the Condition of Intending Fasting Ramadan from the Night Before

ruling.hanafi: Forming the intention at night is not a condition for the fast of Ramadan; it is valid with an intention formed at night or during the day before mid-morning, though the night intention is better.
ruling.maliki: The intention must be formed at night, before dawn breaks or together with it; forming it afterwards is not valid in any fast, obligatory or voluntary.
ruling.shafii: The intention must be formed at night, and an obligatory fast is valid only with an intention before dawn, based on his saying ﷺ: “Whoever does not resolve upon the fast before dawn, there is no fast for him.”
ruling.hanbali: The intention must be formed at night, and an obligatory fast is valid only with an intention formed before dawn breaks.

auto.title: Ruling on Sufficiency of a Single Intention for the Entire Month of Ramadan

ruling.hanafi: A single intention at the start of the month does not suffice for all of it; an intention is required for each day separately.
ruling.maliki: A single intention at the start of the month suffices for the whole month's fast as long as the sequence is not broken by illness or travel, and renewing it each night is recommended.
ruling.shafii: A single intention does not suffice for the whole month; it must be specified for each day on its own.
ruling.hanbali: A single intention at the start of Ramadan does not suffice for the whole month's fast; one is required for each day separately.

auto.title: Ruling on Deliberately Eating and Drinking While Fasting in Ramadan and What It Entails

ruling.hanafi: Whoever deliberately eats or drinks during the day in Ramadan without an excuse invalidates their fast, and they must perform qadaʾ and the major kaffarah (fasting two consecutive months or feeding sixty poor people).
ruling.maliki: Whoever deliberately and willingly eats or drinks in an obligatory fast (like Ramadan) invalidates their fast, and must perform qadaʾ and the severe kaffarah, along with the sin of violating the day.
ruling.shafii: Whoever deliberately eats or drinks during the day in Ramadan invalidates their fast and must perform qadaʾ; the kaffarah is not obligatory for deliberately eating and drinking, but only for sexual intercourse.
ruling.hanbali: Whoever deliberately eats or drinks without an excuse during the day in Ramadan invalidates their fast and must make it up (qadaʾ) and refrain for the rest of the day; the kaffarah is not obligatory upon them, because it is specific to sexual intercourse.

auto.title: Ruling on Smoking and What is Intentionally Inhaled During the Day of Fasting

ruling.hanafi: The fast is invalidated by intentionally drawing smoke or incense into the body cavity, whatever the smoke may be, and qadaʾ is required. Kaffarah is also due for intentionally smoking tobacco, as Ibn ʿĀbidīn reports from al-Shurunbulālī.
ruling.maliki: The fasting person breaks their fast by the arrival of smoke, incense, and all intentionally inhaled substances to the throat and body cavity, and qadaʾ is obligatory upon them.
ruling.shafii: The fast is invalidated by the intentional arrival of any physical substance (such as smoke, incense, and inhaled matter that has substance) into the body cavity through an open orifice.
ruling.hanbali: The fasting person breaks their fast by smoking and intentional inhalation if it reaches the body cavity, because it is a substance reaching the interior by their choice, thereby breaking the fast.

auto.title: Looking at the Woman One Intends to Marry, and How Far It Extends

ruling.hanafi: It is recommended that a suitor look at the woman he seeks to marry, and the looking is confined to the face and the hands: the face shows her beauty, and the hands whether her body is full or spare.
ruling.maliki: It is recommended to look at the face and hands only of the woman one seeks to marry, before the contract, with her knowledge or her guardian's; looking at her unawares is disliked, and nothing else of her body is looked at.
ruling.shafii: It is a sunnah for a suitor to look at the woman before making his offer, even without her leave, and the looking is confined to the face and the hands as far as the wrists, since these are not ʿawrah and by them her good qualities are judged.
ruling.hanbali: It is a sunnah for a suitor to look at the woman he seeks to marry, even without her leave, and he may look at what ordinarily shows of her — the face, the neck, the hands and the feet.

auto.title: Making an Offer of Marriage over Another Man's Offer

ruling.hanafi: It is forbidden to make an offer over another's once the woman or her guardian has inclined to the first man and accepted him; if there was no acceptance, or the first was turned down, it is permitted. And if the contract is made despite the prohibition, it holds, though the man has sinned.
ruling.maliki: It is forbidden to make an offer over another's once the woman has inclined to the first man, even if no dower has been fixed, unless the first withdraws or gives leave. And if the contract is made, it is annulled before consummation by an irrevocable divorce, but not after it.
ruling.shafii: It is forbidden to make an offer over another's once the first man has had an explicit acceptance — on the strength of his saying ﷺ: “Let none of you make an offer over his brother's offer.” If the answer was only a hint, or she kept silent, or the first was turned down, it is not forbidden. And the contract holds if made, though the man has sinned.
ruling.hanbali: It is forbidden to make an offer over the offer of one's Muslim brother once the first man has had an explicit acceptance, or an inclination to him is found; if the first gives leave, withdraws, is turned down, or his position is unknown, it is permitted. And if the contract is made, it holds, though the man has sinned.

auto.title: Offering Marriage to a Woman in Her Waiting Period, Openly or by Hint

ruling.hanafi: Offering marriage openly to a woman in her waiting period is forbidden in every case. Hinting is forbidden to a divorced woman, whether revocably or irrevocably divorced, and permitted to a widow.
ruling.maliki: Offering marriage openly to a woman in her waiting period is forbidden, whatever the kind of waiting period. Hinting is allowed to a widow and to an irrevocably divorced woman, and forbidden to a revocably divorced one.
ruling.shafii: Offering marriage openly to any woman in her waiting period is forbidden. Hinting is permitted to a widow and to an irrevocably divorced woman, since her first husband has no way back to her — unlike the revocably divorced woman, who is still in the position of a wife, so hinting to her is forbidden.
ruling.hanbali: Offering marriage openly to a woman in her waiting period is forbidden in every case. Hinting is permitted to a widow and to an irrevocably divorced woman, and not to a revocably divorced one, since she is a wife whom her husband may still take back.

auto.title: Being Alone with the Betrothed Woman and Travelling with Her before the Contract

ruling.hanafi: Being alone with the betrothed woman and travelling with her are forbidden, for she remains a stranger to her suitor until the contract is concluded; the betrothal adds nothing to the rulings that govern a woman who is a stranger to him, save that it permits the sanctioned looking.
ruling.maliki: Being alone with the betrothed woman and travelling with her are forbidden; she is as any other woman who is a stranger to him until the contract is made over her, and the betrothal is a promise of marriage that permits none of this.
ruling.shafii: Being alone with the betrothed woman and travelling with her are forbidden — on the strength of his saying ﷺ: “Let no man be alone with a woman, for the third of them is Satan.” The betrothed woman is a stranger to him, and the betrothal adds nothing to the rulings that govern a stranger, save that it permits the looking which the betrothal itself calls for.
ruling.hanbali: Being alone with the betrothed woman and travelling with her are forbidden, since the betrothal changes nothing of the rulings that govern a woman who is a stranger to him, save that it permits the looking to one who intends to marry her.
